etymology.text: Pictogram of a person with both hands at the waist; the original meaning was ‘waist’, now written 腰.

funFacts: The character once meant ‘waist’ — when it was borrowed for ‘want’, the flesh radical was added to make a new character 腰.

In 要求 (yāoqiú, ‘to demand’) the character is read yāo (1st tone).
subtleties: 要 is direct: at a counter 我要… is normal; to elders or hosts 我想要… sounds softer.
想 + verb = ‘would like to’ (a wish); 要 + verb = ‘want to, am going to’ (a firmer intention).

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: phonetic 相 (‘to look at’) + semantic 心 (‘heart, mind’) — to visualise, to think. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *saŋ (‘to think’).

funFacts: 心 ‘heart’ is at the bottom of 想: in Chinese tradition the heart is the seat of thought.
pitfalls: 想 needs a verb before a thing: 我想吃土豆 / 我想要土豆. 想 + a person or place means ‘miss’: 我想你 ‘I miss you’.
‘I don’t want to’ is 我不想 — not 我不要 (which sounds like a refusal or a command).
subtleties: 想 = a wish (softer, may not happen); 要 = a firmer intention. 我想去 ‘I’d like to go’, 我要去 ‘I’m going to go’.

etymology.text: 做 ‘to do, to make’ (originally a colloquial variant of 作) + 饭 ‘cooked rice; meal’: ‘to make the meal’.

funFacts: Like Turkish yemek yapmak and Greek φτιάχνω φαγητό, Chinese says ‘make the meal’ — 做饭.
The proverb about the housewife without rice is how Chinese say ‘you can’t make bricks without straw’.
pitfalls: 做饭 already contains its object 饭: say 我做饭 ‘I cook’, but for a dish use 做 + the dish: 做鱼 ‘cook fish’, 做汤 ‘make soup’ (not *做饭鱼).
It is a separable verb: other words can come between 做 and 饭 (做了饭 ‘cooked’, 做什么饭 ‘cook what?’) — this comes later.
subtleties: 做饭 is cooking a meal in general; the technique has its own verb: 炒 ‘stir-fry’, 煮 ‘boil’, 蒸 ‘steam’, 烤 ‘roast, bake’.

etymology.text: 水 ‘water’ + 果 ‘fruit’ (pictogram of fruits on a tree): ‘water-fruit’, juicy fruit.

funFacts: 水果 is literally ‘water fruit’ — the juicy kind; dried fruit and nuts are 干果 ‘dry fruit’.
pitfalls: ‘The fruits of one’s labour’ is 果实 or 成果, never 水果.
一种水果 is ‘a kind of fruit’; 一个水果 ‘one piece of fruit’.
subtleties: Fruit is often served at the end of a meal instead of a sweet dessert.

etymology.text: A shortening of 频婆 (an old Buddhist-era transcription of a Sanskrit fruit name) + 果 ‘fruit’; the grass radical 艹 was added to 頻, giving 蘋.

funFacts: On Christmas Eve, 平安夜 ‘the night of peace’, people in China give each other apples: 苹 píng sounds like 平 píng ‘peace’.
pitfalls: 苹果 can mean an iPhone in conversation: 我的苹果 may be ‘my iPhone’.
Traditional script writes 蘋果; 苹 alone is a different, rare character in traditional texts.
subtleties: In fast speech the second syllable is often light: píngguo.

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 米 ‘rice’ + phonetic 唐. The original meaning was ‘sweet rice cake’ or ‘sugar syrup’.

funFacts: Guests at a Chinese wedding get 喜糖 ‘happy sweets’ — and 什么时候请我们吃喜糖？ ‘When will you treat us to wedding sweets?’ asks when you’ll marry.
pitfalls: 糖 táng (2nd tone) vs 汤 tāng (1st tone) ‘soup’ and 躺 tǎng ‘to lie down’.
吃糖 means ‘to eat sweets’; sugar in a drink is 放糖 ‘put sugar in’ or 加糖 ‘add sugar’.
subtleties: Sugar is a mass noun: it is measured, not counted — 一点儿糖 ‘a little sugar’, 一勺糖 ‘a spoonful’; 一块糖 is a lump of sugar or a sweet.

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: phonetic 監 + semantic 鹵 ‘salt’ (traditional 鹽). From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *g-rjum ‘salt’.

funFacts: Salt was a state monopoly in China for some two thousand years; the Han-dynasty ‘Discourses on Salt and Iron’ (盐铁论) record the debate about it.
pitfalls: 盐 yán (2nd tone) vs 烟 yān ‘smoke; cigarette’ and 眼 yǎn ‘eye’.
The adjective ‘salty’ is 咸 xián: 太咸了 ‘too salty’ — 盐 is only the noun.
subtleties: Salt is measured, not counted: 一点儿盐, 一勺盐 ‘a spoonful of salt’, 一袋盐 ‘a bag of salt’.

etymology.text: Pictogram of flowing water; as a component it is written 氵. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *lwi(j) ‘to flow’.

funFacts: The three dots 氵 on the left of 汤 ‘soup’, 汁 ‘juice’ and 酒 ‘alcohol’ are ‘water’: they mark liquids.
pitfalls: Water is measured by its container: 一杯水, 一瓶水 — not *一个水.
Warm or boiled water (热水, 开水) is a usual drink in China; for cold water say 冰水 or 凉水.
subtleties: 水 can mean money or profit in a few words: 薪水 ‘salary’, 油水 ‘perks’.

etymology.text: From archaic 荼 ‘bitter plant’; possibly borrowed from Proto-Loloish *la ‘tea’ (Sagart) or from an Austroasiatic word for ‘leaf’ (Schuessler).

funFacts: Most languages took their word for tea from Chinese: tea, Tee and Hebrew תֵּה from coastal Min tê; çay, чай, τσάι and Arabic شَاي from chá.
pitfalls: 红茶 ‘red tea’ is what English and German call black tea (Schwarztee); 黑茶 ‘black tea’ is a fermented tea like pu’er.
Tea is counted by the cup or the pot: 一杯茶, 一壶茶.
subtleties: 喝茶 can also mean a relaxed meeting: 有空来喝茶 ‘come over for tea some time’.

etymology.text: A loanword; the word goes back to Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish kahve, from Arabic قَهْوَة qahwa.

funFacts: One word through the learner’s languages: Arabic قَهْوَة → Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → German Kaffee, Greek καφές, Russian кофе — and Chinese 咖啡.
pitfalls: Both characters were made for the sound (口 + a phonetic); 咖 is also read gā in 咖喱 ‘curry’.
Coffee is counted by the cup: 一杯咖啡.
subtleties: 咖啡色 ‘coffee colour’ is a common word for brown.

etymology.text: 牛 ‘cow, ox’ (pictogram of a bull’s head; from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ŋwə) + 奶 ‘milk’: ‘cow’s milk’.

funFacts: 牛 ‘cow’ is also slang for ‘awesome’: 太牛了! ‘amazing!’
pitfalls: 奶 alone is colloquial (and also ‘breast’) and it is part of 奶奶 ‘grandma’: for the drink say 牛奶.
Milk is counted by its container: 一杯 / 一瓶 / 一盒牛奶.
subtleties: Other milks name the animal or the source: 羊奶 ‘goat’s milk’, but soy milk is 豆浆 ‘bean liquid’.

etymology.text: 果 ‘fruit’ + 汁 ‘juice, sap’ (氵 ‘water’ + 十; the origin of the word is unclear).

funFacts: For one fruit the 果 is dropped: 苹果汁 ‘apple juice’, 橙汁 ‘orange juice’ — fruit + 汁.
pitfalls: Vegetable and meat juices are just 汁: 番茄汁 ‘tomato juice’, 肉汁 ‘meat juices, gravy’.
Juice is counted by the glass or the bottle: 一杯果汁, 一瓶果汁.
subtleties: Packaged ‘juice’ is often a 果汁饮料 ‘juice drink’ with little real juice — the label says so.

etymology.text: 葡萄 ‘grape’ (borrowed around 130 BC, perhaps from Bactrian *bādāwa ‘wine’, compare Persian bâde) + 酒 ‘alcoholic drink’ (氵 + phonetic 酉, a wine jar).

funFacts: If 葡萄 really comes from an Iranian word for ‘wine’, then 葡萄酒 is ‘wine-wine’ — the grape reached China along the Silk Road.
pitfalls: 酒 alone is any alcoholic drink, very often Chinese spirits (白酒): for wine say 葡萄酒 or 红酒.
Wine is counted by the glass or the bottle: 一杯 / 一瓶葡萄酒.
subtleties: On the mainland 葡萄 is said pútao, with a light second syllable; Taiwan says pútáo.

etymology.text: 啤 (a character made for the sound, from English beer or German Bier, via Shanghainese) + 酒 ‘alcoholic drink’.

funFacts: Tsingtao (青岛) beer was founded in 1903 by German and British settlers in the German-leased territory of Qingdao — German Bier is behind both the word and the brewery.
pitfalls: 啤 has no meaning of its own: it exists only for the sound pí in 啤酒.
Beer is counted by glass, bottle or can: 一杯 / 一瓶 / 一罐啤酒.
subtleties: Restaurants may serve beer at room temperature: ask for 冰的 ‘a cold one’.

etymology.text: 午 ‘noon’ (the seventh of the twelve earthly branches; originally a pictogram of a pestle) + 饭 ‘meal’.

funFacts: 午 is the hour of the Horse, 11:00–13:00, in the old twelve-hour day; 中午 ‘noon’ and 下午 ‘afternoon’ come from it.
pitfalls: 午饭 is the meal, 中午 the time: 中午吃午饭 ‘have lunch at noon’.
subtleties: After lunch many people take a short nap, 午睡.

subtleties: Dinner in China is often eaten early, around six o’clock.
